title: Don’t Exploit the Window: Washington Asks Sarajevo for Restraint
sources: Washington Agreement on the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (1 March 1994)
content:
The Washington Agreement of 1 March 1994 did more than end the Croat-Bosniak war; it transformed the military balance. With the HVO no longer a hostile front and Croatian supply routes reopening, the ARBiH gained, for the first time, the prospect of concentrating its strength against the Bosnian Serb army rather than fighting on two fronts. The Sarajevo government saw, in the months after Washington, a genuine military window — an opportunity to convert the new Federation’s combined weight into territorial recovery.

The same Western patrons who had brokered the Federation moved quickly to discourage Sarajevo from exploiting it. Their priority was a negotiated settlement that would freeze the lines and end the war on terms the international community could manage — not a Bosniak-Croat offensive that might widen the conflict, draw in Belgrade, or undercut the diplomacy of the newly forming Contact Group. The message to Sarajevo was, in effect, that the military window the patrons had just helped open should not be walked through.

This placed the Bosnian government in a familiar bind in sharpened form. The patrons had delivered a real strategic gain, then asked the beneficiary not to use it. To the Sarajevo leadership, after two years of besiegement and arms embargo, the request to hold back at the precise moment of advantage could look like the international community managing the war toward a frozen partition rather than a just outcome. Yet defying the patrons risked the very support that had made the Federation — and the new military potential — possible.

The decision was thus whether to bank the patron relationship or spend the military opportunity. To acknowledge the call for restraint was to subordinate battlefield possibility to the diplomatic timetable of the powers. To resist it was to assert the government’s right to pursue its war aims with its own newly consolidated forces — at the cost of straining the alliance on which everything still depended.
